content:
The Islamic dilemma is an argument that claims to trap Muslims with their own scripture. The Quran affirms the Torah given to Moses and the Gospel given to Jesus, and it tells the People of the Book to judge by what God revealed in them.[1] So, the Islamic dilemma runs, either those books were intact in the 7th century, which makes our copies reliable and puts them in conflict with the Quran, or they were already corrupt, which means the Quran praised and commanded books no one could follow. Either way, Islam fails. The Islamic dilemma is a fork, preserved or corrupted, and each claim is meant to be fatal on its own.

Two claims, no exit. Tidy, and tidiness is what should make you look closer. A dilemma only works if every third option is properly closed off, and the Islamic dilemma needs 5 separate assumptions to close them. This article is a plain Muslim answer to the Islamic dilemma for general readers. Each entry below names one assumption, says what the Quran and the classical scholars actually say, and gives the strongest form of the reply the other side would make.

What the Islamic dilemma claims, stated fairly

In its current form the Islamic dilemma was popularised by Christian apologists, most prominently David Wood and James White, in debates, lectures and online videos. The Islamic dilemma deserves to be stated at its strongest. The verses the Islamic dilemma usually quotes are 5:47 ("let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein"), 5:68 ("you are [standing] on nothing until you uphold [the law of] the Torah, the Gospel"), 10:94 ("ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you"), 3:3 (the Quran was sent down "confirming what was before it") and 5:48 ("confirming that which preceded it of the Scripture").[1]

Read in a row, as the Islamic dilemma reads them, they can sound like a blanket endorsement of the Bible as Christians held it in Medina. Since the manuscripts of the New Testament long predate Islam, the Islamic dilemma concludes that the Quran endorsed the very texts that contradict its message that God has no son and that Jesus was not crucified. A fair answer to the Islamic dilemma has to deal with every one of those verses, and it has to do so from the classical sources.

The first assumption of the Islamic dilemma concerns names. The Quran talks about the Tawrāt and the Injīl as revelations given to two prophets. The Torah was sent down to Moses, and the Gospel, the evangel, was given to Jesus. Singular. A revelation he received. Verse 5:46 says that God gave him the Injīl, "in which was guidance and light".[1]

Matthew, Mark, Luke and John are narratives about him, written by other people, in a language he did not preach in, and even mainstream critical scholarship dates the earliest of them decades after his death.[2] Jesus spoke Aramaic, and the four books are in Greek. The Quran never names any of them and never counts four. Ibn Ḥazm of Cordoba, who died in 1064, made the point nine centuries before anyone framed the Islamic dilemma: Christians themselves do not claim the Gospels were sent down by God to Jesus, he wrote, but agree that they are "four histories" compiled by four known men at different times.[3] Ibn Taymiyya observed the same difference in transmission: the Torah was carried by a whole people, while the Gospel "was transmitted by four".[4]

Whether the Quranic Injīl refers to those 4 documents is the question the whole Islamic dilemma turns on. The Islamic dilemma does not answer it. It assumes it on the way past. The same distinction between a revelation given to a prophet and later writings about him matters for the letters of Paul, which make up most of the New Testament; the apostleofdoom.org piece on Paul and the Islamic dilemma follows that thread, and our own answer to "Where is the Injil?" sets out the Muslim view of what happened to the Gospel.

The fair objection from defenders of the Islamic dilemma is that seventh-century Christians held the four Gospels, and the Quran tells them to judge by "the Gospel", so it seems to treat what they held as the real thing. The reply is that the Quran refers to what God revealed to Jesus. It does not certify a canon that was settled by church councils, and Muslim scholars have said that echoes of that revelation may survive in human accounts. Ibn Kathir reads 3:3 the same way: the Torah and the Gospel were "guidance for the people" in their own time.[5] Without the first assumption, the Islamic dilemma has no first claim.

The Islamic dilemma runs a binary. Either a text is wholly reliable or it is worthless.

Nothing in the Quranic vocabulary of taḥrīf, meaning distortion, demands that. The Quran describes people concealing much of what they were given (6:91), writing things with their own hands and calling it revelation (2:79), twisting the text with their tongues (3:78), and moving words from their places (4:46).[6] Every one of those verses, which the Islamic dilemma rarely quotes, describes a mixed state. Truth still in there, alteration alongside it.

Against the Islamic dilemma, a scripture in that condition is still worth consulting for what survives in it, which is what an instruction to judge by it would mean. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ gave a rule for exactly this situation. When the People of the Book relate something from their scripture, a Muslim should neither believe it nor reject it outright, and should say that he believes in God and in what was revealed to the believers and to them.[7] That rule makes no sense if the earlier books were pure, and none if they were pure fiction. It fits a mixed text, which is the third option the Islamic dilemma leaves out.

The objection runs that a text which is partly altered gives no means of telling which part. Muslim scholars answered this long before the Islamic dilemma was named. The Quran is the criterion: what agrees with it is accepted, what contradicts it is set aside, and the rest is left in suspense. That criterion is where the Islamic dilemma is weakest, and we return to it under muhaymin below.

Classical exegetes split on this, and the split is old. The two positions have names: taḥrīf al-lafẓ, a change in the wording, and taḥrīf al-maʿnā, a change in the meaning. The Islamic dilemma quietly needs the first to be the only Muslim view. It is not.

Al-Ṭabarī, the early exegete, explains "they distort words from their places" in 4:46 as "they change its meaning and alter it from its interpretation", and reports Mujāhid's gloss that this was the Jews' alteration of the Torah.[8] Ibn ʿAbbās, in a report in al-Bukhari, warns Muslims not to consult the People of the Book because they "changed the book of God and altered it, and wrote the book with their hands".[9] A gloss in one of al-Bukhari's chapter headings goes the other way: no one can remove a word of any of God's books, it says, and the distortion is misinterpretation. Ibn Ḥajar notes that he could not find that gloss traced to Ibn ʿAbbās by a sound chain, and found it instead from Wahb ibn Munabbih.[10] Either way, the view that defeats the Islamic dilemma was held and argued in early Islam.

Ibn Taymiyya, writing his long reply to Christian polemic, summed the debate up. The majority of Muslims, he said, hold that some of the words were changed, as many of the meanings were, while some Muslims hold that the change was in the meanings and not the words. Then he added the line that matters for the Islamic dilemma: on both views, the Quran's confirmation gives no support to the doctrines it rejects, because nothing in the books themselves teaches those doctrines plainly.[11]

Take the second view and the Islamic dilemma simply evaporates: the text stays consultable while its custodians read it wrong. Take the first and the Islamic dilemma still faces the mixed text of the previous entry. The Islamic dilemma, advertised as inescapable, has been answered since the early centuries by positions held inside the tradition.[12] The compelling-evidence.com analysis of the Islamic dilemma takes the same question from the side of the evidence.

The verse the Islamic dilemma quotes sits inside a passage that also calls the Quran muhaymin over what came before it. Quran 5:48: "confirming that which preceded it of the Scripture and as a criterion over it".[1] The proponents of the Islamic dilemma usually quote the first half of that sentence.

Ibn Kathir collects what the early authorities said the word means. Ibn ʿAbbās glossed it as trustee, witness and judge over the books before it, and Mujāhid, Qatāda and al-Suddī said much the same. Ibn Jurayj spelled out what follows: the Quran is the trustee over the earlier books, so whatever in them agrees with it is true, and whatever contradicts it is false. Ibn Kathir concludes that the meanings are close, since a muhaymin is all three at once.[13] That reading predates the Islamic dilemma by centuries.

That is a claim of authority over the earlier books, and the Islamic dilemma has no room for it. So the instruction to the People of the Book, telling them to judge by what they hold, comes from a text that in the same breath sets itself up as the standard their holdings are measured against. Quote the instruction, drop the clause one verse later, and you have manufactured the Islamic dilemma. Put the clause back and it is gone.

The same verse says the Quran confirms what was before it, and the Islamic dilemma leans on that word. Ibn Kathir explains the confirmation in 3:3 and 5:48 as the Quran fulfilling what the earlier books foretold, its own coming among them.[5] The Islamic dilemma treats confirming as endorsing. To confirm a scripture as a kind of revelation is a smaller claim than to endorse every copy in circulation. The lailatulqadar.guide piece on "confirming" and muhaymin looks at the same words through the verses on the Night of Decree.

The verses behind the Islamic dilemma address particular communities in a particular dispute. Several of them concern a legal question the People of the Book brought to the Prophet for judgment, and the reproach is that they were holding a scripture whose ruling they would not apply.

The reports on the occasion of revelation tell of a Jewish couple in Medina who had committed adultery. Their community asked the Prophet to judge, hoping for a lighter penalty than the stoning in their Torah. He asked for the Torah to be read, and when a man covered the verse with his hand it was uncovered, and the Prophet applied the Torah's penalty.[14] The reproach in 5:43, how they make you their judge when they have the Torah with God's ruling in it, belongs to that scene. It shows a ruling that survived in the text, and a community that would not apply it: the mixed state again, which the Islamic dilemma says cannot exist.

The verse on "the people of the Gospel" judging by what is revealed has two canonical readings, and Ibn Kathir gives both. Read one way, it states the purpose of the Gospel: God gave it so that its people would judge by it in their own time. Read the other way, it is a command, and its content is to believe all that was revealed in it, including the good news of a prophet to come. He links it straight to 5:68, where "upholding the Torah and the Gospel" includes following Muhammad, and to 7:157, which says his description is found in their books.[15] On either reading, the verse the Islamic dilemma relies on points Christians towards the Quran, and on neither does it certify a canon. Ibn Kathir also notes that the verse was revealed concerning the Christians, as its context shows.[13]

Then there is 10:94, the verse the Islamic dilemma often treats as decisive. It is a conditional addressed to the Prophet: "if you are in doubt". Ibn Kathir cites Qatāda's report that the Prophet said, "I do not doubt and I do not ask", and he reads the verse as reassurance for the believers that the Prophet's description was in the books the People of the Book held.[16] Asking people who read a scripture about a prophecy in it is a long way from declaring the whole of it intact, which is what the Islamic dilemma needs.

Turning all of this into a timeless endorsement of every manuscript tradition that reached the 21st century is a long stretch. The Islamic dilemma makes the stretch without mentioning that it is making one.

Why the Islamic dilemma fails: the bottom line

For the Islamic dilemma to hold, all 5 assumptions have to hold. The Injīl has to be the 4 gospels. Corruption has to be all or nothing. Distortion has to be textual only. The Quran has to defer to books it calls itself guardian over. And a situational instruction has to be a universal one. Knock out any one of them and the Islamic dilemma has a third option sitting right there: the earlier revelations were real, what survives of them is mixed, and the Quran is the criterion that sorts it.

Most people who push the Islamic dilemma know these responses exist. The real disagreement is narrower and more technical than the marketing suggests, and it is about which reading of taḥrīf the Quranic vocabulary will carry. That is a debate worth having, and the Islamic dilemma, honestly stated, is no trap. If the Islamic dilemma has unsettled you personally, the murtadd.org guide for someone who met the Islamic dilemma online walks through it gently, and our answers on what the Quran says about Christians and on whether a preserved text proves it is true cover the ground around it.

The Islamic dilemma across the network
